newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine not trapped in boom-bust cycle-Ramos.
newsitem.headline: Philippine not trapped in boom-bust cycle-Ramos.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Friday celebrated five years in power by saying there was no danger that the economic boom he helped engineer would start to dull.
"The Philippines is no longer trapped in its old cycle of boom and bust," Ramos said, dismissing fears that Asia's latest would-be tiger economy might slow down.
The fundamental strength of the Philippine economy has not changed, he said in a televised address to the nation on his record since coming to power in 1992.
The Philippine economy is expected to grow by seven percent this year and eight percent next year, compared to almost zero growth before he took office.
"I see this last full year of my term as an opportunity, and a challenge, to consolidate our reform programmes and secure our country's place in the international community," Ramos said.
He has repeatedly denied he will run for a second term in next year's presidential polls despite pressure from supporters to amend the constitutional limit on a president to a single six-year term.
The constitution was rewritten 10 years ago to include the limit following the 20-year rule of late dictator Ferdinand Marcos.

"Our achievements over the past five years are rooted in policies of pragmatism which reversed the protectionist and inward-looking policies that have hobbled the economy (and) dismantled the monopolies and cartels that have stifled competition."
Ramos said his administration has cut crime.

"If we have made decisive gains in moving the economy forward -- banishing once and for all our reputation as the sick man of Asia -- that is partly because of the climate of better peace and order we have established in our country," he said.
The challenge for development lies ahead as trade walls among countries are starting to crumble.
"Competition in the global economy has become so intense that we must run just to stay in place," Ramos said.
"We no longer should be satisfied with leapfrogging, for others are leapfrogging too. Rather, our aim should be to pole-vault into the 21st century," he said.

"Our free and open society is a competitive advantage in itself that foreign investors and our neighbours acknowledge and even applaud, because freedom stimulates creativity in the individual and the whole society."
